header:
Gold, explained:
why it hits records

lines.text: Gold pays zero. Why did central banks buy 863 tonnes?
lines.say: Gold pays zero. Why did central banks buy eight hundred sixty-three tonnes?

lines.text: That was in 2025, when gold set 53 record highs, says the World Gold Council.
lines.say: That was in twenty twenty-five, when gold set fifty-three record highs, says the World Gold Council.

lines.text: The top came in late January 2026: about $5,590 an ounce.
lines.say: The top came in late January twenty twenty-six: about five thousand five hundred ninety dollars an ounce.

lines.text: Then it slid. By November 18, 2026, spot gold was near $3,720, a third below January's record.
lines.say: Then it slid. By November eighteenth, twenty twenty-six, spot gold was near three thousand seven hundred twenty dollars, a third below January's record.

lines.text: And central banks kept buying: 675 tonnes in the first nine months of 2026.
lines.say: And central banks kept buying: six hundred seventy-five tonnes in the first nine months of twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: So why does a metal that pays nothing keep hitting records, and why does it crash?
lines.say: So why does a metal that pays nothing keep hitting records, and why does it crash?

lines.text: Here's the plan: gold as money, who buys it, what moves it, and what it costs.
lines.say: Here's the plan: gold as money, who buys it, what moves it, and what it costs.

lines.text: Quick note: this is education, not financial advice, and no price predictions.
lines.say: Quick note: this is education, not financial advice, and no price predictions.

lines.text: Chapter 1: how gold became money.
lines.say: Chapter one: how gold became money.

lines.text: Gold is rare, it never rusts, and you can melt it into small pieces that all look the same.
lines.say: Gold is rare, it never rusts, and you can melt it into small pieces that all look the same.

lines.text: That's why, for centuries, it was money itself, or the thing paper money promised to swap for.
lines.say: That's why, for centuries, it was money itself, or the thing paper money promised to swap for.

lines.text: In 1934, the US Gold Reserve Act raised gold's official price from $20.67 to $35 an ounce.
lines.say: In nineteen thirty-four, the US Gold Reserve Act raised gold's official price from twenty dollars and sixty-seven cents to thirty-five dollars an ounce.

lines.text: In 1944, the Bretton Woods system tied other currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold.
lines.say: In nineteen forty-four, the Bretton Woods system tied other currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold.

lines.text: Foreign governments could trade $35 for one ounce. But pressure built, and in 1971 the US shut that window.
lines.say: Foreign governments could trade thirty-five dollars for one ounce. But pressure built, and in nineteen seventy-one the US shut that window.

lines.text: On August 15, 1971, President Nixon told the country what he had done.
lines.say: On August fifteenth, nineteen seventy-one, President Nixon told the country what he had done.

scene.text: I have directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets

lines.text: He said he'd directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold.
lines.say: He said he had directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold.

scene.text: I have directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets

lines.text: Temporarily turned out to be forever. By 1973, the major currencies were floating, according to the State Department's historians.
lines.say: Temporarily turned out to be forever. By nineteen seventy-three, the major currencies were floating, according to the State Department's historians.

lines.text: Since then, a dollar is backed by trust in the US, not by gold. And gold's price floats freely.
lines.say: Since then, a dollar is backed by trust in the United States, not by gold. And gold's price floats freely.

lines.text: Chapter 2: booms, busts and records.
lines.say: Chapter two: booms, busts and records.

lines.text: Once it floated, gold ran: from $35 in 1971 to $850 at the London fix on January 21, 1980.
lines.say: Once it floated, gold ran. It went from thirty-five dollars in nineteen seventy-one to eight hundred fifty dollars at the London fix on January twenty-first, nineteen eighty.

lines.text: That's about 24 times higher in under nine years, by our math.
lines.say: That's about twenty-four times higher in under nine years, by our math.

lines.text: Here's gold's yearly average price, every five years, from 1970 to 2025, based on LBMA prices.
lines.say: Here's gold's yearly average price, every five years, from nineteen seventy to twenty twenty-five, based on London market prices.

lines.text: In 1980, the yearly average was about $615. Then came a slump that lasted about 20 years.
lines.say: In nineteen eighty, the yearly average was about six hundred fifteen dollars. Then came a slump that lasted about twenty years.

lines.text: By 2000, the average was down to about $279. Gold had lost more than half its price.
lines.say: By the year two thousand, the average was down to about two hundred seventy-nine dollars. Gold had lost more than half its price.

lines.text: And in 2025, the average hit about $3,431, up 44% in one year, per the World Gold Council.
lines.say: And in twenty twenty-five, the average hit about three thousand four hundred thirty-one dollars, up forty-four percent in one year, according to the World Gold Council.

lines.text: The very bottom of that long slump came in mid-1999, near $252 an ounce.
lines.say: The very bottom of that long slump came in mid nineteen ninety-nine, near two hundred fifty-two dollars an ounce.

lines.text: Part of the reason: European central banks were selling. In September 1999, they agreed to cap sales at 400 tonnes a year.
lines.say: Part of the reason: European central banks were selling. In September nineteen ninety-nine, they agreed to cap sales at four hundred tonnes a year.

lines.text: Remember: in the 1990s, central banks were sellers. In the 2020s, they're the buyers.
lines.say: Remember: in the nineteen nineties, central banks were sellers. In the twenty twenties, they're the buyers.

lines.text: Then came another boom and bust. Gold peaked near $1,920 in September 2011.
lines.say: Then came another boom and bust. Gold peaked near one thousand nine hundred twenty dollars in September twenty eleven.

lines.text: The yearly average went from about $1,669 in 2012 to about $1,160 in 2015, a drop of about 30%, by our math.
lines.say: The yearly average went from about sixteen hundred sixty-nine dollars in twenty twelve to about eleven hundred sixty in twenty fifteen, a drop of about thirty percent, by our math.

lines.text: And after inflation, the 1980 peak wasn't beaten until 2025, Bloomberg reported. That's about 45 years.
lines.say: And after inflation, the nineteen eighty peak wasn't beaten until twenty twenty-five, Bloomberg reported. That's about forty-five years.

lines.text: Then 2025 happened: gold rose about 65% for the year, its best year since 1979.
lines.say: Then twenty twenty-five happened. Gold rose about sixty-five percent for the year, its best year since nineteen seventy-nine.

lines.text: Chapter 3: who buys all this gold?
lines.say: Chapter three: who buys all this gold?

lines.text: Start with the total. In 2025, world gold demand hit a record 5,002 tonnes, worth about $555 billion.
lines.say: Start with the total. In twenty twenty-five, world gold demand hit a record five thousand and two tonnes, worth about five hundred fifty-five billion dollars.

lines.text: Four big groups buy it: jewelry shoppers, people buying bars and coins, funds called ETFs, and central banks.
lines.say: Four big groups buy it: jewelry shoppers, people buying bars and coins, funds called E T Fs, and central banks.

lines.text: Here's what central banks bought each year from 2020 to 2025, in tonnes, from World Gold Council data.
lines.say: Here's how much gold central banks bought each year from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-five, in tonnes, from World Gold Council data.

lines.text: In 2020, they bought about 255 tonnes, the lowest in a decade, during the pandemic.
lines.say: In twenty twenty, they bought about two hundred fifty-five tonnes, the lowest in a decade, during the pandemic.

lines.text: In 2022, it jumped to about 1,082 tonnes, and stayed above 1,000 for three straight years.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-two, it jumped to about one thousand eighty-two tonnes, and it stayed above a thousand for three straight years.

lines.text: Even 2025's 863 tonnes is far above the 2010 to 2021 average of 473 tonnes a year.
lines.say: Even twenty twenty-five's eight hundred sixty-three tonnes is far above the twenty ten to twenty twenty-one average of four hundred seventy-three tonnes a year.

lines.text: And it didn't stop. In the third quarter of 2026, central banks bought 321 tonnes, up 42% from a year earlier.
lines.say: And it didn't stop. In the third quarter of twenty twenty-six, central banks bought three hundred twenty-one tonnes, up forty-two percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: One steady buyer is China's central bank. It reported adding gold for 24 straight months through October 2026.
lines.say: One steady buyer is China's central bank. It reported adding gold for twenty-four straight months through October twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Here's the twist: the World Gold Council estimates about 63% of third-quarter buying wasn't reported by any country.
lines.say: Here's the twist: the World Gold Council estimates about sixty-three percent of third-quarter buying wasn't reported by any country.

lines.text: The biggest official pile is still America's, about 8,133 tonnes. Germany holds about 3,350, and China reported about 2,306 at the end of 2025.
lines.say: The biggest official pile is still America's, about eight thousand one hundred thirty-three tonnes. Germany holds about three thousand three hundred fifty, and China reported about two thousand three hundred six at the end of twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Why do central banks want it? Gold isn't anyone's debt, it can't be printed, and you can keep it in your own vault.
lines.say: Why do central banks want it? Gold isn't anyone's debt, it can't be printed, and you can keep it in your own vault.

lines.text: In a 2026 World Gold Council survey, a record 45% of central banks said they plan to add gold.
lines.say: In a twenty twenty-six World Gold Council survey, a record forty-five percent of central banks said they plan to add gold.

lines.text: Investors piled in too. In 2025, gold ETFs added 801 tonnes, and people bought 1,374 tonnes of bars and coins.
lines.say: Investors piled in too. In twenty twenty-five, gold E T Fs added eight hundred one tonnes, and people bought one thousand three hundred seventy-four tonnes of bars and coins.

lines.text: China and India are the giants. In 2025, bar and coin buying rose 28% in China and 17% in India, while jewelry fell 25% and 24%.
lines.say: China and India are the giants. In twenty twenty-five, bar and coin buying rose twenty-eight percent in China and seventeen percent in India, while jewelry fell twenty-five and twenty-four percent.

lines.text: High prices scared off jewelry buyers by weight, to a five-year low. But spending on jewelry still hit a record $172 billion.
lines.say: High prices scared off jewelry buyers by weight, to a five-year low. But spending on jewelry still hit a record one hundred seventy-two billion dollars.

lines.text: Chapter 4: what moves the price.
lines.say: Chapter four: what moves the price.

lines.text: There are four big levers. The first, and often the biggest, is real interest rates.
lines.say: There are four big levers. The first, and often the biggest, is real interest rates.

lines.text: A real rate is the interest rate minus inflation. For example, 4% minus 3% is a 1% real rate.
lines.say: A real rate is the interest rate minus inflation. For example, four percent minus three percent is a one percent real rate.

lines.text: Gold pays nothing. So $10,000 in savings at 4% earns $400 a year, while $10,000 of gold earns $0.
lines.say: Gold pays nothing. So ten thousand dollars in savings at four percent earns four hundred dollars a year, while ten thousand dollars of gold earns zero dollars.

lines.text: When real rates fall, that missed $400 shrinks, so gold is cheaper to hold. When they rise, gold costs more to hold.
lines.say: When real rates fall, that missed four hundred dollars shrinks, so gold is cheaper to hold. When they rise, gold costs more to hold.

lines.text: Lever two is the US dollar. Gold is priced in dollars all over the world.
lines.say: Lever two is the US dollar. Gold is priced in dollars all over the world.

lines.text: A weaker dollar means an ounce costs more dollars, and gold gets cheaper for buyers using euros or yuan.
lines.say: A weaker dollar means an ounce costs more dollars, and gold gets cheaper for buyers using euros or yuan.

lines.text: In 2025, the dollar index fell about 9.4%, its worst year since 2017. Gold had its best year since 1979.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, the dollar index fell about nine point four percent, its worst year since twenty seventeen. Gold had its best year since nineteen seventy-nine.

lines.text: Lever three is fear. In wars, crises and panics, people want something that isn't anyone's promise.
lines.say: Lever three is fear. In wars, crises and panics, people want something that isn't anyone's promise.

lines.text: In the 2008 financial crisis, the yearly average rose about 25%. In the 2020 pandemic, about 27%, by our math.
lines.say: In the twenty oh eight financial crisis, the yearly average rose about twenty-five percent. In the twenty twenty pandemic, about twenty-seven percent, by our math.

lines.text: Lever four is inflation worries: if people expect money to buy less later, some reach for gold.
lines.say: Lever four is inflation worries. If people expect money to buy less later, some reach for gold.

lines.text: In 2025, the levers lined up: the Fed cut rates three times, the dollar fell, fear was high, and central banks kept buying.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, the levers lined up. The Fed cut rates three times, the dollar fell, fear was high, and central banks kept buying.

lines.text: But levers can also fight each other, and that's what happened in late 2026.
lines.say: But levers can also fight each other, and that's what happened in late twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: In mid-November 2026, gold hit its lowest level in over a year as traders bet the Fed would raise rates.
lines.say: In mid-November twenty twenty-six, gold hit its lowest level in over a year, as traders bet the Fed would raise rates.

lines.text: Higher US rates make gold's zero interest look worse, and a strong dollar added to the pressure.
lines.say: Higher US rates make gold's zero interest look worse, and a strong dollar added to the pressure.

lines.text: Inflation fears were rising too, thanks to oil. The rate lever simply won.
lines.say: Inflation fears were rising too, thanks to oil. The rate lever simply won.

lines.text: So gold isn't a simple inflation switch. It's a tug of war, and the winner changes.
lines.say: So gold isn't a simple inflation switch. It's a tug of war, and the winner changes.

lines.text: Chapter 5: owning gold, and the risks.
lines.say: Chapter five: owning gold, and the risks.

lines.text: There are three common ways people own gold. First, the physical stuff: bars and coins.
lines.say: There are three common ways people own gold. First, the physical stuff: bars and coins.

lines.text: Physical gold costs more than the spot price. That extra is called the premium.
lines.say: Physical gold costs more than the spot price. That extra is called the premium.

lines.text: Premiums change daily. For a 1 ounce American Eagle coin, dealer premiums often run about 3% to 8% over spot.
lines.say: Premiums change daily. For a one ounce American Eagle coin, dealer premiums often run about three to eight percent over spot.

lines.text: Our math: say the premium is 5%. At $3,720 spot, that adds $186, so the coin costs about $3,906.
lines.say: Our math: say the premium is five percent. At three thousand seven hundred twenty dollars spot, that adds a hundred eighty-six dollars, so the coin costs about three thousand nine hundred six.

lines.text: If a dealer later buys it back at spot, gold has to rise about 5% just to break even, plus any storage costs.
lines.say: If a dealer later buys it back at spot, gold has to rise about five percent just to break even, plus any storage costs.

lines.text: Second, gold ETFs: funds that hold gold in a vault and trade like a stock.
lines.say: Second, gold E T Fs: funds that hold gold in a vault and trade like a stock.

lines.text: They charge a yearly fee called an expense ratio. As of 2026, GLD charges 0.40% and GLDM charges 0.10%.
lines.say: They charge a yearly fee called an expense ratio. As of twenty twenty-six, G L D charges zero point four percent, and G L D M charges zero point one percent.

lines.text: Our math: put $10,000 in each and hold for 10 years, with gold's price flat.
lines.say: Our math: put ten thousand dollars in each and hold for ten years, with gold's price flat.

lines.text: At 0.40% a year, fees eat about $393. At 0.10%, about $100. Same gold, same years.
lines.say: At zero point four percent a year, fees eat about three hundred ninety-three dollars. At zero point one percent, about one hundred. Same gold, same years.

lines.text: That's about a $293 gap from the fee alone. Small percentages add up.
lines.say: That's about a two hundred ninety-three dollar gap, from the fee alone. Small percentages add up.

lines.text: Third, mining stocks. Here you're buying a company, not the metal itself.
lines.say: Third, mining stocks. Here you're buying a company, not the metal itself.

lines.text: Miners' profits move with gold, and some pay dividends. But they add company risks: costs, debt, and mines that disappoint.
lines.say: Miners' profits move with gold, and some pay dividends. But they add company risks: costs, debt, and mines that disappoint.

lines.text: Now the risks, plainly. One: gold has no yield. No interest, no dividends, no rent. Its only return is the price.
lines.say: Now the risks, plainly. One: gold has no yield. No interest, no dividends, no rent. Its only return is the price.

lines.text: Two: long slumps. Bought at the 1980 peak, it took about 28 years just to get back to $850.
lines.say: Two: long slumps. Bought at the nineteen eighty peak, it took about twenty-eight years just to get back to eight hundred fifty dollars.

lines.text: Three: big swings. Even after all those records, it can fall fast.
lines.say: Three: big swings. Even after all those records, it can fall fast.

lines.text: From about $5,590 in January to about $3,720 in November 2026 is a drop of about 33%, by our math.
lines.say: From about fifty-five hundred ninety dollars in January to about thirty-seven hundred twenty in November twenty twenty-six is a drop of about thirty-three percent, by our math.

lines.text: That's the trade-off. Gold can zig when other things zag, but it can also sit flat or fall for decades.
lines.say: That's the trade-off. Gold can zig when other things zag, but it can also sit flat, or fall, for decades.

lines.text: Chapter 6: the recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: One: gold was money, then the backing for money, until 1971. Since then, its price floats.
lines.say: One: gold was money, then the backing for money, until nineteen seventy-one. Since then, its price floats.

lines.text: Two: central banks flipped from sellers to big buyers, about 863 tonnes in 2025 alone.
lines.say: Two: central banks flipped from sellers to big buyers, about eight hundred sixty-three tonnes in twenty twenty-five alone.

lines.text: Three: the price mostly follows real rates, the dollar, fear and inflation worries.
lines.say: Three: the price mostly follows real rates, the dollar, fear and inflation worries.

lines.text: Four: owning it costs money. Our coin needed a 5% gain to break even, and the pricier ETF cost about $393 over 10 years.
lines.say: Four: owning it costs money. Our coin needed a five percent gain to break even, and the pricier E T F cost about three hundred ninety-three dollars over ten years.

lines.text: Five: no yield, long slumps, and big swings, like that drop of about a third.
lines.say: Five: no yield, long slumps, and big swings, like that drop of about a third.

lines.text: So gold hits records when the levers line up, and it falls hard when they flip.
lines.say: So gold hits records when the levers line up, and it falls hard when they flip.

lines.text: None of this says where gold goes next. It just explains why it moves.
lines.say: None of this says where gold goes next. It just explains why it moves.

lines.text: That's the money. Follow for more.
lines.say: That's the money. Follow for more.

post.title: Gold pays zero interest. So why do central banks keep buying it, and why does it crash?
post.ig: Gold pays zero interest, yet central banks bought 863 tonnes in 2025. Here's why it hits records and why it falls.
post.tiktok: Gold pays zero interest. Central banks bought 863 tonnes anyway. Here's why.
post.yt_desc:
Gold pays no interest, yet it set 53 record highs in 2025, peaked near $5,590 an ounce in January 2026, and then fell about a third by November 2026. This video explains gold from zero: how it went from money to the backing for money until 1971, its long booms and busts, who buys it (central banks bought 863 tonnes in 2025, per the World Gold Council), and the four levers that move its price: real interest rates, the dollar, fear and inflation worries. We also work through the real costs of owning it, with our math on a coin premium and on ETF fees over 10 years, plus the risks.

CHAPTERS

Sources: World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends Full Year 2025 (Jan 29, 2026) and Q3 2026 (Nov 3, 2026); WGC Central Bank Survey (June 2026); Reuters via Nation Thailand, Khaleej Times and NST gold market reports (Nov 12-18, 2026); Federal Reserve History, Gold Reserve Act of 1934; US State Department Office of the Historian, Nixon and the End of Bretton Woods; Nixon address (Aug 15, 1971); Bloomberg (Sept 11, 2025; Dec 31, 2025); BullionVault (Dec 31, 2025); MetalCharts and NMA LBMA annual averages; ETF.com fund fee comparison (2026); USAGOLD and dealer premium trackers (Nov 2026); PBOC/SAFE reserve data via China Daily HK (Nov 2026); IMF/WGC official gold reserves (Dec 2025).

News and education, not financial advice.
